title: A Strongly Subcubic Combinatorial Algorithm for Triangle Detection with Applications

predicted_errors.error_location: k-Clique application section (paragraph beginning 'Obtaining faster than trivial...')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper cites Abboud, Fischer, and Schechter [3] (arXiv:2401.13502, Jan 2024) as already having announced 'A slightly faster combinatorial algorithm' for k-clique. However, later in the same section the paper claims 'thereby providing the first solution to the above open problem' (obtaining faster-than-trivial combinatorial algorithms for k-clique by more than polylogarithmic factors). These two statements are internally inconsistent: either [3] already provided the first solution, or this paper's solution is the first — both cannot be true simultaneously without clearer qualification distinguishing what [3] achieved vs. what is claimed here.

The core algorithm component BFS^+ (modified BFS) is never formally defined. The paper states 'we will use the following slightly modified version of BFS with a start vertex s' and then references 'Step 12 of the modified BFS procedure and Fig. 1(i)' — but the BFS^+ pseudocode is never provided in the text, nor is Step 12 explicitly defined. The triangle detection logic is described only through a case analysis (Cases 1, 2.1, 2.2) and Figure 1 illustrations. While the case analysis is fairly complete, the absence of the BFS^+ pseudocode means the algorithm specification is technically incomplete — a reader cannot implement the algorithm without inferring the BFS^+ details from the case analysis.

predicted_errors.error_location: Definitions and notations section and k-Clique application
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states as a default assumption: 'Unless specified otherwise: (i) all algorithms discussed are assumed to be deterministic.' Yet the paper's central contribution is a randomized algorithm, and the paper claims to 'strongly invalidate' the combinatorial k-clique conjecture. Many formulations of the combinatorial k-clique conjecture in the cited literature [3, Conj. 2], [12, Hypothesis 1.1] refer specifically to deterministic combinatorial algorithms. The paper does not clearly distinguish whether its claimed invalidation applies to the deterministic or randomized version of the conjecture, creating ambiguity about the scope of its main claim.

summary:
The paper presents a randomized combinatorial algorithm for triangle detection claiming O(n^{7/3}) time, which would be a landmark result if correct. The core mathematical analysis — including the probability bound (exp(-70) ≤ 10^{-30}), the time complexity derivations (O(n^{7/3}) for triangles, O(n^{25/9} log n) for BMM, O(n^{7k/9}) for k-clique, O(1.715^n) for Max-Cut), and the case analysis — appears internally consistent and free of provable algebraic errors under lenient scrutiny. The Boolean product equation and closed-neighborhood definition are standard and correct. The K₄ runtime optimization (O(m^{15/8}) with x = m^{7/16}) balances correctly.

Three issues were identified that warrant review:

1. (Confidence 0.82) The paper both acknowledges [3] as prior work solving faster combinatorial k-clique AND claims to provide 'the first solution' — an internal inconsistency in the narrative.

2. (Confidence 0.75) The BFS^+ procedure — the central algorithmic component — is never formally specified with pseudocode, relying instead on a case analysis and figure references. While the case analysis is fairly complete, the algorithm specification is technically incomplete.

3. (Confidence 0.70) The claim to invalidate the combinatorial k-clique conjecture may be overstated if the conjecture was intended for deterministic algorithms, which is the typical interpretation in fine-grained complexity literature.

No mathematical errors were detected in equations or derivations. The paper's central time complexity claims are internally consistent with their stated assumptions. The missing BFS^+ pseudocode and the 'first solution' narrative inconsistency are the most significant concerns and should be addressed before publication.
